cells.tense: Present — you're here, hand on the work.
cells.verb: wearing down what stands between people until it gives
cells.place: in how close you actually let yourself get to someone
cells.ask: take one connection you've been patiently reshaping and look at it plainly, like a craftsman studies a joint — what moved, when, after what — so the next one can be done with less effort and the time alone with it feeds you instead of walling you off.
cells.core:
You're changing how things sit between you and someone, and you're doing it the slow way — not a speech, not a scene, just showing up again with the same steady pressure until the old shape gives. It's working. Walls that stood a long time are coming down without anyone being knocked over, and the people on the other side still feel like themselves when it's done.

That's rare: real change in a relationship that doesn't cost the relationship. What this is free to feed next is a little method. Take one connection you've been patiently reshaping and look at it plainly — what moved, when, after what — the way a craftsman studies a joint that held. Not to doubt it. So the next one costs less, and the time you spend alone with it connects you to people rather than keeping you from them.
cells.sheetLine: You're changing how things stand between you and people, slowly, and it's holding.

cells.tense: Future — you're already living in the version where they've finally changed.
cells.verb: forcing the change between you before anyone's ready for it
cells.place: in how close you actually let yourself get to someone
cells.ask: tell one person what this change means to you — the story of it, not the plan — and let them take whatever part of it is theirs; what comes back is that the things that give way are the ones that needed to, and nothing else.
cells.core:
You're pressing on how things stand between you and someone, and the pressing has gotten ahead of the person. Somewhere ahead there's a version where they've finally moved, finally understood, finally rearranged themselves the way you can see they could — and you're already living there, so every ordinary moment with them becomes a shove toward it. They can feel the shove. It's hard to be close to someone who's renovating you.

The weight of this is real; you can see what would be better and it's slow. But the thing you're reaching for isn't the rearranging — it's the closeness it was supposed to make room for. Try the other door. Tell one person what this change means to you — the story, not the plan — and let them take whatever part of it is theirs and leave the rest. What comes back when you're steady again is that the things that give way between you are the ones that needed to, and the rest stands.
cells.sheetLine: You're renovating the relationship faster than the person in it can move.

cells.tense: Past — the moment to push is behind you and you're still standing there.
cells.verb: letting what stands between you stay standing
cells.place: in how close you actually let yourself get to someone
cells.ask: decide one clear thing in your own life — a boundary, a plan, a line — and act on it today, not aimed at anyone; when your own ground is clear, the pushing comes back on its own, and what needed to fall between you starts to fall.
cells.core:
There's something between you and someone that's been there a while, and you've stopped working on it. You know its shape exactly. At some point the steady pressure you're capable of went quiet, and now you sit beside the person with the wall in place, calling it patience or respect or just how it is. It's none of those. It's a door you were about to go through, and didn't, and you're still at it.

The tool isn't to try harder at the wall. Pushing on a relationship from empty just makes noise. Charge the other side of yourself instead: decide one clear thing in your own life — a boundary, a plan, a line you'll hold — and act on it today, not aimed at anyone. When your own ground is clear and things make sense around you, the steady push comes back on its own, and what needed to fall between you starts to fall.
cells.sheetLine: You can see the wall exactly. You stopped leaning on it.

cells.tense: Disowned present — you're writing this and calling it the weather.
cells.verb: quietly rebuilding how things stand between you
cells.place: in how close you actually let yourself get to someone
cells.ask: name the one thing you actually want from a connection you've been quietly reshaping, say it once to yourself without an excuse attached, and keep wanting it on purpose; what comes back is change that comes from what you really see, and the things that fall are the ones that needed to.
cells.core:
You're already changing how things stand between you and someone — steadily, over months, in a hundred small refusals and returns — and you'd tell anyone it just happened that way. Things evolved. People drift. But the drift has a direction, and the direction is yours. You can feel yourself choosing it every time the subject comes up, and you keep describing it as something that's being done to both of you.

It's working, which is why it's worth owning. Go back to the simpler thing under it. Name the one thing you actually want from this connection — say it once to yourself without an excuse attached — and keep wanting it on purpose, the way you'd tend a small fire so it doesn't go out and doesn't burn the house. Once the wanting has your name on it, the change starts coming from what you really see, and what falls between you is only what needed to.
cells.sheetLine: You're already rebuilding this. You're calling it drift.
